statements.claim: The rasa dance took place on a full-moon autumn night on the Yamuna bank at Vrindavan.
Krishna began the rasa dance and the gopis of Vraja gathered around him.
Krishna multiplied himself to stand between every pair of gopis, so each felt him near her alone.
The circle was bright with bangles, anklets and little bells keeping time.
The gopis' earrings swung against their cheeks, their throats flushed as they sang, and their hair came loose with flowers slipping from it.
One gopi sang with Krishna in a single blended voice; another, weary, leaned on his shoulder; one kept only anklet and girdle tinkling as she sang.
The gopis shone in the ring like lightning within a circle of clouds.
The women of the sky looked on bewildered, and the gods rained flowers down on the dance.
As the night wore on the gopis grew tired, some assuming a show of pride while still singing of his deeds and delighting in the touch of his hands.
Krishna led them to the river to wash away the heat of the dance; in the water they splashed him and he took his ease among them.
In this way the moonlit autumn nights passed, one after another.

notes: Tightly faithful to BP 10.33.1-24; every sensory detail (bangles/anklets/bells, earrings, red throats, loosened hair, the three individual gopis, lightning-in-clouds simile, celestial women, flower-rain, pride-and-song, splashing in the water) has a direct Sanskrit antecedent. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Akrura was sent to Vrindavan to bring Krishna and Balarama to Mathura, where Kamsa reigned and their parents waited worn down by the king's cruelty.
At the Yamuna, Akrura stopped the chariot, stepped down to wash while the brothers waited, sipped water bright as a gem, and sank beneath the surface murmuring the eternal prayer (brahma sanatana).
Under the water he first saw the two sons of Vasudeva still seated in the chariot as he had left them, and surfaced in confusion before diving again.
He then beheld Ananta, the lord of serpents, with a thousand heads and a thousand hoods, being praised by those around him.
Resting in the serpent's coils was a figure dark as a rain-cloud, in yellow silk, serene and smiling, holding lotus, conch, discus and mace, adorned with crown, bracelets and armlets.

Attendants Sunanda and Nanda, the sages Sanaka and his brothers, and devotees Prahlada and Narada stood by, with goddesses of fortune, nourishment, speech, beauty, fame, contentment, strength and glory in attendance.
He rose trembling with joy and praised the Lord with a voice choked with feeling.
The Bhagavata presents the serpent Ananta bearing the dark Lord (not Balarama as the serpent); the telling follows the Bhagavata.

notes: Faithful to BP 10.39.37-56. The two-stage dive, maṇi-prabham ('bright as a gem') water, Ananta's thousand heads/hoods, the dark Lord's attributes, the named attendants and goddesses, and the choked praise all match the Sanskrit. The variant (Harivamsha/VP making Balarama the serpent) is correctly disclosed in tradition_note. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Kubja, named 'the three-bent one' (Trivakra), was a servant favored by Kamsa whose work was the making of his unguents/sandal paste.
Krishna and Balarama, having just entered Mathura in Akrura's chariot, walked the city's broad highways like two young elephants let loose from their posts.
Krishna asked who she was and for whom the paste was meant; she answered it was for the king but that the two of them deserved it more, and anointed them with her own hands.
Pleased, Krishna pressed down her feet with his feet and lifted her head with two fingers beneath her chin, straightening her crooked body into a beautiful woman.
She begged him to come to her house, saying she could not bear to let him go, and he promised to come after finishing his work in the city.
She is described as small and poor and unnoticed by the crowd.

notes: Faithful to BP 10.42.1-12. The straightening gesture (feet pressing her feet, two fingers under the chin) is precisely BP 10.42.6, not the Harivamsha 'haunch' variant; the 'two young elephants' and crimson evening-sun details trace to Harivamsha 1.82 (listed as an additional source). 'Small and poor' is a mild connective inference from her servant status, not a factual claim needing correction.

statements.claim: Kamsa set his champions Chanura and Mushtika against the two boys before the packed assembly.
The match was hand-to-hand, foot-to-foot, elbow-to-elbow and knee-to-knee, with whirling, throwing and grappling; the verses call it a contest of equal against equal.
The women protested the unequal match, calling the wrestlers hard as diamond in every limb like mountains against the two boys, and praising the fortune of Vraja and the gopis' penance.
Krishna sprang at Chanura with a hawk's speed, both fists clenched, struck, and Chanura did not flinch — the blow falling like a garland on an elephant.
Krishna then seized Chanura, whirled him and dashed him to the ground, and his life left him.
Balarama slew Mushtika, and then Kuta fell to Balarama, Shala to a blow from Krishna's foot, and finally Tośala.

notes: Faithful to BP 10.44.1-27. The wrestling grips, the women's full protest speech, the hawk-strike/garland-on-elephant simile, and the sequence Chanura, Mushtika, Kuta, Shala, Tośala all match the Sanskrit verbatim. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: After the champions fell, Kamsa ordered the two sons of Vasudeva driven from the city, Nanda bound, and Vasudeva put to death.
Enraged, Krishna sprang onto the high dais before Kamsa could rise; Kamsa reached for his sword while Krishna moved like a hawk sweeping left and right.
Krishna seized Kamsa by the hair so that the crown shook loose, dragged him from the seat and hurled him into the arena, then fell upon him and dragged his body before all the people.
Kamsa had lived in constant dread, seeing Krishna in everything — drinking, eating, walking, sleeping, breathing — the prophecy of his death by Devaki's child following him everywhere.
They had come to Mathura to set their parents free (as Uddhava recalls in BP 3.2.34).

notes: Faithful to BP 10.44.28-38 and 3.2.34. The orders (expel the sons, bind Nanda, kill Vasudeva — as per the evidence summary), the sword/hawk simile, the hair-seizing with loosened crown, and the 'seeing Krishna in drinking/eating/walking/sleeping/breathing' dread all match. The 'prophecy' framing is inherent to the source's dread motif. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: After finishing their studies, Krishna and Balarama asked their teacher Sandipani what fee he would take, having learned the whole Veda at his feet.
Sandipani, after consulting his wife, asked as his fee the return of his young son who had died in the sea at Prabhasa.
The brothers drove their chariot to Prabhasa; the ocean, knowing who had come, rose and brought them an offering.
The ocean said the boy was not in its keeping but had been carried off by the demon Panchajana, who lived in the waters in the form of a conch shell.
Krishna entered the water, slew Panchajana, and took from his body the great conch shell known to the world as Panchajanya.
He drove to the city of Yama, blew the conch, and Yama came out and honored them with deep reverence, returning the boy.
The boy was restored in his former person and returned to his father, who blessed the brothers: 'Go home, heroes, and may your fame be pure.'

notes: Faithful to BP 10.45.36-47 (plus 3.3.1, Harivamsha 1.88, VP 5.21). The Prabhasa setting, the wife-consultation, the ocean's offering, Panchajana-as-conch ('tad-aṅga-prabhavaṃ śaṅkham'), the blowing of the conch at Yama's city, and Sandipani's 'gacchataṃ sva-gṛhaṃ vīrau kīrtir vām astu pāvanī' all match. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: A foreign king (Kalayavana/Yavana) marched on Mathura with an enormous foreign army, and Jarasandha's forces would arrive once battle began, so Krishna would face two armies at once.
Krishna chose a site in the sea and asked the ocean to withdraw its waters over a stretch twelve yojanas wide.
On an auspicious day under a favorable star, he made offerings to the brahmanas and had them perform benedictory rites.

He summoned Vishvakarma, the divine architect, in his mind, and the architect built Dwaraka — a sea fortress twelve yojanas wide with high ramparts, silver-and-gold turrets, gardens of celestial trees and vines, and skillfully laid courtyards.
Indra sent the Sudharma assembly hall and the Parijata tree; Varuna sent swift white horses.
By his mystic power Krishna conveyed all the people — the whole Yadava clan with their families and goods — from Mathura to the new city.

He told the Yadavas the site was like the very abode of the gods and the city would be named Dwaravati, as Indra's city is Amaravati; he laid out courtyards, promenades and roads, and gave each family land.
Temples were raised for the gods in proper places, four great gates were built, and the Yadavas marked their plots with ropes and measured their streets.

notes: Faithful to BP 10.50.42-56 and Harivamsha 1.115. The twelve-yojana sea site, ocean-withdrawal request, Rohini-star auspicious day with brahmana offerings, Vishvakarma summoned in the mind, Sudharma+Parijata from Indra, white horses from Varuna, the yoga-prabhāvena conveyance, and the Dwaravati/Amaravati naming all have direct source support. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Rukmini was the princess of Vidarbha, daughter of Bhishmaka, king of Kundina.
Krishna had asked for her hand but her brother Rukmin, who hated him, refused; at Jarasandha's suggestion her father affianced her to Sisupala.
Krishna came to Kundina with Balarama and many Yadus, while the allied kings of Sisupala had gathered for the wedding.
Rukmini went to the temple to pray and, coming out, the assembled princes were struck still by her beauty, some slipping from their seats on elephants, horses and chariots.
She pushed back a strand of hair with her left hand and glanced shyly over the princes, and her eyes found Krishna.
Krishna set her on his chariot bearing the Garuda banner and drove through the ring of kings like a lion carrying off his share from the midst of jackals.

The proud kings (Jarasandha and the rest) cried that their bow-won fame had been snatched by cowherds, like a lion's kill stolen by deer; Rukmin swore never to return to Kundina until he had slain Krishna.

Rukmin overtook the chariot; Krishna scattered his army as if in sport and flung him to the ground, and Rukmini begged for her brother's life — 'He is my only brother... Give him to me' — and Krishna spared him.
Rukmin kept his vow, founded the city Bhojakata and dwelt there ever after; Krishna married Rukmini in due form, and she bore Pradyumna, a portion of the god of love.

notes: Faithful to BP 10.53.52-56 for the seizure and VP 5.26 for the background and Rukmin's defeat, exactly as the tradition_note discloses. The left-hand hair-push and shy glance, Garuda-banner chariot, lion-vs-jackals and deer-stealing-lion's-kill similes, Rukmin's vow, Rukmini's plea, Bhojakata's founding, and Pradyumna's birth all have direct source support. No unsupported or contradicted claims.
